project_goal: Create an original score-driven 2D arcade destruction game in which players convert momentum into destruction and destruction rewards back into momentum through increasingly skillful routing, progression, and repeat leaderboard attempts.
target_users: Players who enjoy route optimization and repeated mastery attempts
Casual players who want immediately understandable controls with a high skill ceiling

mvp.summary: A complete offline-first Windows arcade game built in Godot with one truck, three fixed-layout levels, two building types, ground and aerial routing, Survival and Timed Efficiency modes, compact progression, local achievements/statistics, and anonymous online leaderboards.
must_have: Windows PC build using Godot and GDScript
2D side-view gameplay with 2D physics
One truck with timing-based launch, always-available capped mid-air rotation, and limited directional nudge energy
Survival mode with no hard time cap and a typical successful run target of 5–8 minutes
Timed Efficiency mode using the same core physics and content with separate rules and leaderboards
One standard difficulty
Three fixed-layout levels selected and tuned from development-time generated candidates
One ground-level building layer and an aerial opportunity layer
Two data-driven building types with binary intact/destroyed states
Any truck contact destroys an intact building and removes a fixed amount of speed
One simple collidable wreck shape per destroyed building; smaller debris is visual only
Balloon targets and a compact set of rare aerial momentum opportunities
At least one special momentum-granting building variant using shared building behavior
Composite scoring based on destruction value plus distance, chains, bounces, and launch accuracy
Money tied primarily to destruction value
Permanent upgrades, a swappable rear equipment slot, and several temporary run boosts
Radar progression from crude warnings to useful route-planning information
Offline gameplay, progression, saves, achievements, statistics, and unlocks
Anonymous online per-level leaderboards with Stock and Progression categories
Compact run records and server-side plausibility validation rather than deterministic physics replay
Queued offline leaderboard submissions
One local profile with safe atomic save replacement and one automatic backup
Up to 10 local achievements
A compact single-screen statistics page
Keyboard and gamepad support through a unified mobile-aware action abstraction
Essential accessibility and settings options
One-time contextual hints instead of a dedicated tutorial
Functional, fast menus and optional Instant Restart
English-only launch text implemented through a localization-ready system
Compact gameplay-focused art, VFX, and audio scope
Opt-in automatic crash reporting
Developer-only debug tools excluded from public release builds
Downloadable Windows build, recorded gameplay proof, manual acceptance checklist, and automated tests for non-visual core logic
postponed: Full accounts, authentication, cloud saves, profiles, and synchronized cross-device progression
Multiple local profiles and save-slot management
Replay recording, playback, sharing, and replay-driven anti-cheat
Photo mode and automatic highlight capture
Daily or weekly challenges, seasons, live events, and live-operations systems
Official mod support, custom content APIs, and Workshop integration
Dynamic weather, day/night variants, and seasonal presentation
Adaptive soundtrack, announcer, and cinematic audio
Cinematic menus, animated garage scenes, story, lore, dialogue, and cutscenes
Large cosmetic catalogues and animated cosmetic effects
Social profiles, friends, chat, and rich player histories
Public pre-launch roadmap or committed season plan
Novelty cheat codes, which may only be considered later with achievements and leaderboard submissions disabled

stack.recommendation: Use Godot and GDScript for the Windows MVP, while keeping controls, UI scaling, performance budgets, and data contracts compatible with a later Android port.

options.name: Godot with GDScript
options.best_for: Rapid 2D arcade prototyping, data-driven gameplay, cross-platform packaging, and an AI-heavy implementation workflow.
risks: Arcade physics feel requires extensive playtesting and tuning
Network/backend services remain separate engineering concerns
Performance budgets must be enforced for later Android support

notes: The repository is initialized and uses the AI Assembly Line repository-first lifecycle.
Accepted requirements, planning, task decomposition, and implementation are separated by pull-request gates.
The product must remain an original spiritual successor and must not copy proprietary code, names, art, audio, branding, or level layouts.

tools.name: AI Assembly Line
tools.configuration: Repository-first lifecycle with separate requirements, planning, and task-decomposition pull requests.
tools.notes: Merged repository artifacts are authoritative; chat context is temporary.

team_mode.parallelization_goal: Optimize for a flexible AI-heavy team with approximately 4–6 concurrent implementation agents, potentially supervised by two humans using the project at the same time. Define contracts and file ownership before parallel work.

working_style.review_style: Evidence-first review with a dedicated AI integration role. Contributors have local autonomy inside accepted subsystem contracts; the project owner resolves remaining ties. No contributor may silently move clearly post-MVP scope into the MVP.
proof_required: Automated tests for deterministic non-visual core logic
Benchmarks or focused prototypes when technical approaches conflict
Clear PR-level evidence for acceptance criteria

constraints: Protect the MVP aggressively; small-looking additions still require explicit scope approval.
Prototype every gameplay mechanic with placeholder assets before final art or polish.
Prefer reusable data-driven content over bespoke scripts.
Prioritize predictable arcade feel and player understanding over physical realism.
Permanent progression should expand planning, control, and tactical options rather than replace skill.
All gameplay and progression must remain available offline.
Internet use is limited to leaderboard retrieval/submission, opt-in crash reports, and a possible update check.
Gameplay rules, scoring, and physics remain equivalent across visual quality profiles.
Menus prioritize speed and function over spectacle.
The complete game is free to play; monetization is cosmetic-only or voluntary support.
No randomized paid rewards or gambling-like cosmetic mechanics.
No official replay, analytics, modding, live-ops, or social ecosystem in the MVP.
Planning must support 4–6 concurrent AI implementation agents with explicit contracts, dependencies, and file ownership.
Evidence beats opinion; when technically equivalent, fun wins.
safety_boundaries: Family-friendly cartoon destruction only: no blood, visible injured people, realistic suffering, or graphic consequences.
Do not copy proprietary assets, source code, names, branding, audio, or level layouts from the inspiration.
Every external asset must have its source, author, license, permitted use, and attribution requirement recorded before inclusion.
Paid or supporter content must never change physics, scoring, progression power, resources, unlock requirements, leaderboard eligibility, or competitive advantage.
Crash reporting must be opt-in and exclude save files, screenshots, gameplay recordings, personal information, and continuous telemetry.
Public release builds must not expose developer cheats or debug controls.
assumptions: Godot provides suitable 2D physics, input abstraction, Windows packaging, and later Android support.
Two building types and a small aerial object set are sufficient to prove the core loop before content expansion.
A simple authored wreck collider produces enough post-impact immersion without physical debris affecting competitive runs.
Fixed speed subtraction per destroyed building can be tuned into a readable resource-routing economy.
Compact run validation can reject obviously impossible leaderboard submissions without proving every run legitimate.
A dedicated AI integration role can assist multiple human contributors while preserving human approval authority.
Exact numerical balancing values, upgrade prices, thresholds, and content counts inside accepted caps will be determined through prototypes and playtesting during planning and implementation.
acceptance_signals: The launch, bounce, destruction, aerial recovery, and retry loop is fun with debug graphics and placeholder UI.
Players can understand momentum costs and improve their routes through practice.
Ground and aerial opportunities create meaningful recurring decisions without passive dead time.
Typical successful Survival runs cluster around 5–8 minutes while expert runs can continue beyond that without a hard cap.
Timed Efficiency offers a clearly distinct competitive objective without duplicating the physics or content stack.
Progression and radar upgrades expand tactical planning without eliminating the need for skill.
The three fixed levels, one truck, two building types, and compact object set feel like a complete game rather than a technology demo.
The Windows build runs reliably, saves safely, supports offline play, and submits eligible leaderboard records when connected.
Automated tests pass for scoring, progression transactions, save/load behavior, and compact run-record validation.
Human reviewers accept the requirements/bootstrap pull request as the authoritative MVP boundary.
